The playback core is a headless background process that handles decoding, audio output, and the D-Bus control interfaces. start launches it in the background and returns immediately; foreground runs it in the current terminal; stop, restart, status, and reload manage an existing instance. Only one primary instance may own the bus name; --force starts an extra instance on a secondary bus name. Secondary instances do not accept regular commands and must be addressed with --bus <name> (placed after the subcommand).
{prog} daemon start {prog} daemon status {prog} daemon stop
Load this path and start playback after starting or restarting (this process scans it and pushes the queue)
Enable debug logging to daemon.log in the configuration directory
Force the operation: allow a secondary instance, or terminate a running TUI
Also act on every secondary instance (stop only)
Do not start playback automatically; wait for a front end to deliver a queue (foreground only)
Print the full status snapshot as JSON (status only; same as show --json)
Start the playback core in the background

The core detaches from the terminal, and the command returns as soon as its bus name is online. Without --open it starts an idle core and waits for a front end to deliver a queue; with --open the core starts first, then this process scans the path, delivers the queue, and starts playback. If a primary instance is already running, startup is refused unless --force is given, which starts a secondary instance. Inside a sandbox, D-Bus activation is requested instead.
Load this path and start playback after the core starts (this process scans it)
Write debug logs to daemon.log in the configuration directory
Start a secondary instance even if a primary instance already exists
Run the playback core in the foreground in the current terminal

The core keeps the current terminal attached until it receives a termination signal or is stopped with daemon stop; this suits systemd, tmux, and similar supervisors. The core does not scan directories: --open is reported and ignored, and the queue still comes from a front end. If a primary instance is already running, startup is refused unless --force is given, which runs it as a secondary instance.
No longer applicable: the core does not scan directories; it is reported and ignored
Write debug logs to daemon.log in the configuration directory
Run as a secondary instance when the primary bus name is taken
Do not start playback automatically; wait for a front end to deliver a queue

Stops the core gracefully and waits up to 5 seconds for its bus name to be released. A core hosting a TUI is not terminated unless --force is given. --all also stops every secondary instance started with --force; it can clean them up even when no primary instance is running.
Allow terminating a core that hosts a TUI

Stops the existing instance gracefully (waiting up to 10 seconds), then starts a new core in the background. A running TUI requires --force. With --open, the core starts first, then this process scans the path, delivers the queue, and starts playback.
Load this path and start playback after restarting (this process scans it)
Write debug logs to daemon.log in the configuration directory
Allow terminating a core that hosts a TUI and restart it
Show the status of the playback core
Prints the instance mode and PID, followed by a one-line playback status; any secondary instances are also listed on stderr. --json prints the complete Info.GetInfo JSON snapshot instead.
Print the complete JSON snapshot (same as show --json)
Make the core reload its configuration
Asks the running core to re-read config.xml and apply settings that can be updated at runtime, such as info display and volume. An instance must be running.
Inspect and modify the current playback queue
The queue is scanned and delivered by a front end and owned by the core; these subcommands inspect or modify the live queue over D-Bus. All subcommands require a running playback core.
{prog} queue list {prog} queue append ~/Music/a.flac,~/Music/b.flac {prog} queue insert 0 ~/Music/c.flac
List the queue contents page by page

Shows the total number of entries, the current track, and the page start, then prints position, title, artist, and path per row; the current track is marked with >. offset is zero-based; count 0 uses the core default page size of 200, with a maximum of 1000.
Show at most N entries (0 = default 200, maximum 1000)
Removes every entry from the queue; it prints nothing on success and returns a non-zero exit code if the core refuses.
Keeps the current track first and shuffles the remaining entries. It prints nothing on success.
Remove the entry at a given position
Positions are zero-based; out-of-range positions are rejected by the core.
Append tracks to the end of the queue

Accepts one or more local track paths, separated by commas or passed as multiple arguments; each path becomes one queue entry and directories are not expanded. On success it prints the number of entries added.
Insert a track after a given position
Positions are zero-based and the new track is inserted after that position; out-of-range positions are rejected by the core. The path must be a local track, and directories are not expanded.
Inspect and modify the running core's configuration

Reads and writes the configuration of the running instance. set applies immediately and writes config.xml; reload re-reads the file; reset restores built-in defaults. All subcommands require a running playback core.
{prog} config get volume_percent {prog} config set volume_percent 65 {prog} config reset --yes
Read a configuration value or the full configuration

Without a key it prints the full configuration JSON; with a key it prints only that scalar value (for example ui_language or volume_percent), and version is also available. The key must be a scalar field in the configuration schema; composite sections such as equalizer are not supported.

Parses the value according to the key's schema type: strings are stored as-is, while integers and floats are validated as numbers. Changes apply immediately and are written back to config.xml; unknown keys or type errors are rejected as a whole.
Asks the core to re-read config.xml from disk and apply it; equivalent to daemon reload.
Overwrites the current configuration with built-in defaults and writes config.xml. To prevent accidents, --yes is mandatory; without it the command refuses and changes nothing.
Show the lyrics of the current track
By default it prints the current lyric line and, when available, the next one; --lines N prints up to N timestamped lines instead. If no lyrics are available, it says so.
Print up to N timestamped lyric lines (omit to show only the current line context)
Show the metadata of the current track
Prints the title, artist, album, track number, queue position, and file path; it reports when nothing is playing. This command takes no options.
Print the current track cover as character art

Fetches the current cover from the core and prints it verbatim. Unspecified dimensions come from the configuration; width ranges from 4 to 40 columns and height from 2 to 20 rows. If there is no cover, it says so.
Cover width in columns (4-40; defaults to configuration)
Cover height in rows (2-20; defaults to configuration)
Character set: braille, ascii, or half (defaults to configuration)

list prints actions, labels, and effective keys by context, and reports keys that a child context shadows from its parent; check reads the raw overrides in config.xml and looks for invalid entries, duplicate actions, same-context conflicts, missing default keys, and missing terminfo capabilities. Both only read the configuration and do not require a running playback core.
Print JSON output (list: actions and shadows; check: counts, errors, and warnings)
List the current keys for every action

Prints action IDs, labels, and effective keys grouped by context; overridden actions show their default keys, and non-bindable actions are marked as locked. Shadowing relationships are listed at the end.
Check the key configuration and report problems

Compares the defaults with the raw overrides in config.xml and reports unknown actions, invalid keys, duplicate actions, same-context conflicts, missing default keys, and missing terminfo capabilities. Errors make the exit code 1; warnings alone do not affect it.
